title: Firestone Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Firestone wells have a 25 ft median depth, but local records range to 790 ft. See yields, water levels, risks and estimated costs.
h1: Firestone, Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Firestone means looking beyond the listing’s claim that it has a well. Records within 5 miles show a very shallow local median depth, but the range is wide. Most wells report useful production, and the measured water level is generally close to the surface. That does not remove the need to check the individual permit, well construction, pump equipment, water quality and legal right to use the water.

This page uses Colorado DWR permit records for Firestone and nearby areas including Frederick, Mead, Dacono, Platteville, Longmont and Berthoud. The records include older wells as well as permits issued as recently as 2026, so they are a useful local starting point rather than a guarantee for one lot.

sections.heading: Firestone well depth depends on the formation
sections.html:
The median reported well depth around Firestone is 25 feet. The middle half runs from 15 to 65 feet, and 81% of reported wells are under 100 feet. That is a different drilling picture from a mountain subdivision, but it does not mean every lot will have a shallow, inexpensive hole.

The record reaches 790 feet, with 9% of wells between 100 and 300 feet and 10% between 300 and 600 feet. The local geology is Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, while permits also name unnamed or fractured-bedrock and alluvial aquifers. A driller’s bid should be based on the target aquifer, nearby completions and the planned use, not only the median.

sections.heading: What Firestone wells produce
sections.html:
Only 183 wells in the records report a pump yield, so treat the production statistics as local guidance rather than a promise for an unbuilt well. Among those reports, the median yield is 14.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute.

Forty-seven percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 46% fall from 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Seven percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and none are recorded under 1 gallon per minute. A household well with a storage tank may work well at a lower pumping rate. Confirm the permit’s allowed use; an exempt household-use well also has a 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Firestone’s shallow water level looks stable
sections.html:
Of the records that report a static water level, the median depth to water is 9 feet. The middle half is 6 to 15 feet below the surface. That shallow water level can simplify pumping, but it also means the wellhead, casing, grout and surface drainage deserve close inspection.

The decade figures do not show a dropping table in this dataset: the median was 9 feet below surface in the 2010s and 8 feet in the 2020s. Those are measurements from different wells and dates, not a continuous monitoring record. A buyer should still request the well’s own static level and pumping information, especially where irrigation, stock use or nearby development could affect conditions.

sections.heading: Permit history shows continuing Firestone drilling
sections.html:
Firestone’s permit history is not limited to older rural homes. The records show 36 permits in the 1950s, 53 in the 1960s, 158 in the 1970s, 82 in the 1980s, 200 in the 1990s, 384 in the 2000s, 287 in the 2010s and 431 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026.

Most records identify the driller as Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 643 wells. A. E. Crandall & Sons (Williams, G C) appears on 75, and Clement, Glenn A. on 44. These names help when tracing local construction patterns, but the permit and completion report for the specific property matter more than a contractor’s historical count.

sections.heading: A Firestone well may cost less to drill than to finish
sections.html:
For Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, the modeled drilling rate is $50 to $70 per foot. At the 25-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone is about $1,200 to $1,800. That is only the borehole portion of the job, not a usable water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,200 to $13,800 at the median depth. A shallow median does not make every project fall at the low end: casing, grout, access, difficult ground, permits, pump sizing and the distance to the house can change the bid. Compare proposals by asking what is included and what happens if the planned depth does not produce water.

sections.heading: Firestone buyers should check water quality and site constraints
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 1,496 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 29 historic mine features and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not prove a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to test the property’s water and review nearby land uses before closing.

Low-yield and dry-hole risk still exists despite the reported yield distribution. Ask for the well construction report, pump test, treatment history and recent laboratory results. Check septic setbacks, replacement-area options, drainage, access for a rig and the proposed building location. A well permit is not automatically an approval for every household, irrigation or stock use. Over-appropriated basins may also require an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: Use the Firestone records before you choose a lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare nearby permits by depth, aquifer, use and reported yield. The 25-foot local median is encouraging for drilling estimates, but the 790-foot record shows why a buyer should not budget from one statistic alone. Have a Colorado driller review neighboring completions before signing a construction contract.

For an existing home, make the sale contingent on reviewing the permit, inspecting the pressure system and testing the water. For a new build, confirm the water right, septic layout, electrical route and access for construction equipment together. Ask for a written drilling allowance, a dry-hole or inadequate-yield policy and a finished-system price. That process turns the local data into a site-specific decision.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Firestone, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Firestone is 25 feet, and the middle half runs from 15 to 65 feet. About 81% are under 100 feet. Depths are not uniform, however: the record reaches 790 feet, with wells also reported from 100 to 600 feet and beyond.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Firestone?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate for Firestone’s Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock is $50 to $70 per foot. At the 25-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $1,200 to $1,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $7,200 to $13,800.

faq.q: How much water does a Firestone well produce?
faq.a: Among the 183 local records that report a pump yield, the median is 14.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-seven percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 7% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Firestone?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Within about 10 miles, records map 1,496 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 29 historic mine features and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory and review treatment history before relying on it.

faq.q: Are Firestone well water levels going down?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a decline: static water level was 9 feet below surface in the 2010s and 8 feet in the 2020s. Those figures come from different reported wells, with 197 records listing a static level, so they are not a continuous trend for every Firestone property.
